module: Module 1: How Pay Works at Brunswick
title: How Pay Ranges Are Built

Statement_01.text: The midpoint represents market-competitive pay for someone performing well in the role.

Statement_02.text: People near the top of a range typically have many years of sustained high performance and specialized skills.

Statement_03.text: Ranges also vary by location — across countries, and across zones within the U.S.

Impact_01.text: Being below midpoint is not a signal that something is wrong.

narration.text: So where does a pay range come from? It's not invented — it's built, using a consistent process. The process starts with a job description outlining the role's responsibilities, required skills, and expected contributions. That description is used to benchmark against similar roles in the compensation surveys previously referenced — the same surveys used by hundreds of other companies. Based on this benchmarking exercise, the role is assigned a grade, and each grade has a defined pay range — a minimum, midpoint, and maximum — built from the combined market value of the roles in the grade for that country or location. The midpoint represents market-competitive pay for someone performing well in the role. And it's worth knowing that market-competitive pay isn't a single point — it's a range around the midpoint, which means competitive positioning can sit below the midpoint as well as above it. Being below midpoint is not a signal that something is wrong; it most often reflects someone newer to the role or still building skills and tenure. People near the top of a range typically have many years of sustained high performance and specialized skills. Ranges also vary by location, because costs of labor differ by geography — across countries, and across zones within the U.S. The same grade in an urban area may carry a different pay range than in a rural location. That's not a fairness question — it's a reflection of different labor markets.
